one_liner: Multi-threaded HTTP reverse-proxy cache programmed in VCL; beats a single-worker nginx proxy_cache but not nginx on all cores.
what_it_does: Varnish sits in front of one or more HTTP origin servers and serves cached responses from memory (or a file-backed store), fetching from the backend only on a miss. Behaviour is configured in VCL, a domain-specific language whose subroutines (vcl_recv, vcl_backend_response, vcl_deliver and so on) decide what is cached, for how long and how headers are rewritten. It is a standalone server (varnishd plus varnishlog, varnishncsa and other tools), not a library, and is not a drop-in for nginx's configuration. The GitHub repository was archived on 16 Feb 2026; the project continues as Vinyl Cache at code.vinyl-cache.org.
how_it_is_fast: VCL is translated to C and compiled with the system C compiler into a dlopen(3)-loaded object (cc_command parameter), so request policy runs as native code rather than being interpreted. Cached objects are looked up through a critbit tree (default -h critbit) and stored in the malloc stevedore by default (jemalloc on Linux builds), so hits are served from memory. Requests run on pooled worker threads (thread_pools default 2, thread_pool_min 100, thread_pool_max 5000), idle keep-alive connections are parked in an epoll/kqueue/event-ports waiter, and logging goes to a shared-memory ring (VSL) read by separate tools instead of being written synchronously.
when_to_use: HTTP reverse-proxy caching for sites or APIs where per-request cache logic (normalising URLs, stripping cookies, grace and ban/purge rules) is easier to write in VCL than in nginx directives.

Small cached objects served at high request rates from RAM, on a box where Varnish can use several cores; in the nuster benchmark it sustained about 107-133k req/s for 12 B to 1 KB objects on a 12-core Xeon X5650.
Origins that are slow relative to the cache, where collapsing concurrent misses and serving stale content during refresh matters more than raw hit throughput.
Teams that already run nginx or HAProxy for TLS termination and want a separate, scriptable cache layer behind it.
when_not_to_use: Maximum small-object hit throughput per box: nginx proxy_cache with worker_processes auto beat Varnish 4.1.8 in every row of the only comparison found (for example 214,217 vs 133,094 req/s for a 12-byte body over 1 Gbps).
When you need TLS termination in the cache itself: the core has no TLS listener, so you need Hitch, HAProxy or nginx in front.
When you want HTTP/2 without extra configuration: HTTP/2 is a feature bit (feature=+http2) that is off in the default feature set.
When you need a key-value cache API for application data: it only speaks HTTP to clients and backends.
If you need a single long-term upstream: the GitHub repo is archived, and the code lives on as Vinyl Cache while Varnish Software keeps the Varnish Cache name, so packaging and naming are in flux.

integration.form: standalone server (varnishd plus CLI tools); VMODs as loadable modules
integration.dependencies: libpcre2-8, python3-docutils (rst2man) and python3-sphinx to build, jemalloc by default on Linux, optional libunwind; a C compiler at runtime to compile VCL
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll waiter), FreeBSD and other kqueue systems, Solaris/illumos (event ports, umem storage); macOS has build handling in configure.ac
integration.thread_safety: not applicable: a multi-threaded server process with per-pool worker threads; thread_pools, thread_pool_min and thread_pool_max are runtime parameters

gotchas: Defaults are not tuned for benchmarks: the compared Varnish ran with default thread settings while nginx was given worker_connections 1000000 and keepalive_requests 100000, so neither side was tuned the same way.

The miss-path delay quoted from issue #1923 (30-40 ms extra per miss on 4.0.2) was not a Varnish defect: the reporter traced it to a Node.js backend that sent no Content-Length header, and adding one removed the wait.

Security fixes keep landing in HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 parsing (VSV00014 to VSV00017, HTTP/2 rapid reset CVE-2023-44487 and 'Made You Reset'), so track the Vinyl Cache release stream rather than the frozen GitHub 'last' tag.
vsl_space (default 80M) sizes the shared-memory log; if it is too small varnishlog and varnishncsa cannot keep up.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings is an HTTP reverse-proxy cache: Pogocache, Dragonfly, Valkey and CacheLib are key-value caches or libraries, and AdaptSize is an admission-control patch evaluated on top of Varnish itself. Pick Varnish when the cache must speak HTTP to clients and origins and you want programmable policy; pick a KV cache when the application controls lookups.
verified_claims_summary: The author of the competing nuster cache ran wrk (-t 100, -c 1000 or 5000, 30 s) against Varnish 4.1.8 (malloc 1024M, default threads) and nginx 1.12.2 proxy_cache on a 12-core Xeon X5650 with CentOS 7.4 packages (no compiler or flags stated): Varnish served 2.4-4.0x more requests/s than nginx with one worker, but only 0.62-0.96x of nginx with all 12 workers, which won every row. The 512 B and 1 KB rows over 1 Gbps are close to link saturation for the fastest servers (about 0.89-0.93 Gbit/s of HTTP payload for nginx on 12 workers, derived from page data), and the loopback runs put wrk's 100 threads on the same 12 cores as the server.
status_note: GitHub repository archived on 16 Feb 2026 (last 8.0.0 release 15 Sep 2025, 'last' tag); development continues under the Vinyl Cache name at code.vinyl-cache.org (search snippets mention a 9.0.0 release in April 2026, not opened), and BSD-2-Clause licensing makes it freely deployable.
